summary:
Malaysia criminalises both same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity at two levels, and Kedah stands under that national framework. Sections 377A and 377B of the federal Penal Code punish "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" for any person regardless of gender or consent, carrying a maximum of 20 years plus whipping; these provisions are not limited to Malaysians and apply to visitors. Every one of the 13 states and the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya additionally maintains a Sharia enactment criminalising cross-dressing or "a man posing as a woman", with penalties of up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. Those state offences reach Muslims only.

Kedah's own instrument is the Syariah Criminal Offences (Kedah Darul Aman) Enactment 2014 (En.18/2014). Section 26 criminalises a male posing as a woman in public, punishable by a fine of up to RM1,000 or up to one year's imprisonment. Female cross-dressing is not an offence under the enactment. Like the other state enactments, it contains no legal definition of what constitutes transgender dressing, leaving the scope of the offence to the enforcing officers.

The same Kedah enactment criminalises same-sex conduct between Muslims. Section 23 covers liwat (sodomy) and section 24 musahaqah (lesbian sex), each punishable by a fine of up to RM5,000, up to three years' imprisonment, up to six strokes of whipping, or any combination of those penalties. A woman convicted of musahaqah may additionally be committed to an approved home for up to six months under section 52.

Enforcement in Kedah has targeted transgender people as a category rather than as incidental participants. In October 2020 a private birthday party was raided and 30 transgender women were singled out from the gathering and arrested, while the event's organiser was separately investigated for "encouraging vice". A coalition of Malaysian human-rights groups publicly protested the investigation, identifying a pattern of punishing organisers and allies of transgender persons rather than only transgender people themselves.

For a non-Muslim foreign visitor the Kedah Sharia offences do not apply, but the federal Penal Code does. Enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely targeted; the documented national pattern is raid-based arrest and public outing rather than individual stops.
tangentialFactors:
Kedah's cross-dressing penalty is lighter than the ceiling that applies elsewhere. Section 26 tops out at one year and RM1,000, against the three years, RM5,000 and six strokes of caning available under cross-dressing provisions in other states, and Kedah does not bar women from posing as men, which three states do.

Litigation has narrowed the state layer without loosening the federal one. The High Court denied a request to declare the Sharia prohibition on cross-dressing unconstitutional, and the Federal Court struck down Selangor's section 28 in February 2021 and 16 Kelantan Sharia provisions in February 2024 on federalism grounds, leaving Penal Code offences fully intact. A constitutional challenge was pending as of late 2014 following the mass arrest of 16 trans women at a wedding on 8 June 2014.

Enforcement against gender nonconformity is active and public. In July 2020 the Religious Affairs Minister announced that the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department (Jawi) had his "full licence to carry out its enforcement actions" against transgender persons, an order the International Commission of Jurists demanded be revoked. In the Nur Sajat case, 122 religious officers were mobilised to pursue her for "insulting Islam" before she fled to Thailand and received UNHCR protection.

Queue-and-venue raids carry acute exposure risk for foreign visitors. On 28 November 2025 police raided a male-only sauna in Chow Kit, Kuala Lumpur, arresting 208 men under section 377B in the largest operation of its kind since 2022. Media were pre-tipped and detainees' faces and personal details were leaked; 17 civil servants identified among them were suspended. A magistrate rejected the remand extension as lacking ground, yet release was delayed, with more than 130 people held at one point including 31 foreign nationals whose embassies intervened. Justice For Sisters mobilised bailors and legal aid; on 2 December the Home Minister floated revisiting the provisions, and days later police raided another sauna in Penang.

Trans people in Malaysia face lethal violence and official indifference to it. A transgender woman was killed in Klang on 25 June 2019, the third killing of a trans woman in the country in fewer than two months; documentation of that case records police mistreatment and impunity under the heading "The Deceased Can't Speak for Herself".

The wider climate is one of state-backed restriction. Islamist opposition has foreclosed reform prospects, government-funded mukhayyam "rehabilitation" retreats had drawn 1,733 attendees by June 2021, and LGBT events and media content are censored. There is no same-sex marriage and no anti-discrimination law.
localsOnly:
Muslim residents of Kedah carry exposure under both layers at once: the federal Penal Code and, on top of it, the Syariah Criminal Offences (Kedah Darul Aman) Enactment 2014. Sections 23 and 24 reach consensual same-sex conduct between Muslims in private as well as in public, and section 52 permits a woman convicted of musahaqah to be committed to an approved home for up to six months in addition to the fine, imprisonment and whipping available under section 24.

Section 26 reaches public presentation only, and only for men: a male posing as a woman in public is an offence, while female cross-dressing is not. Because the enactment defines neither term, a resident's exposure turns on how enforcing officers read her appearance rather than on any statutory test.

Enforcement is carried out by the state Islamic religious department, which operates alongside the federal religious enforcement apparatus described in the national record. Residents have no statutory protection against discrimination on grounds of gender identity or sexual orientation, no access to recognition of a same-sex partnership or marriage, and no legal route to change identity documents to match gender presentation under the Sharia layer.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the Kedah 2014 enactment has been challenged in court, or whether any of its sections have been struck down, is not sourced in the material available here; the litigation record cited above names Selangor and Kelantan only.

The frequency of section 26 enforcement within Kedah is unresolved. The October 2020 party raid is the only Kedah-specific enforcement incident in the available material, and its judicial outcome, including the result of the "encouraging vice" investigation, is not sourced.

Whether federal Penal Code prosecutions under sections 377A and 377B have been brought in Kedah, and against whom, is not sourced. The national raid pattern documented in the available material comes from other states and cannot be assumed to describe Kedah.

Practical detail for visitors on the ground in Kedah, including the presence and location of any venues, the posture of local police toward foreign nationals, and consular reporting on the state, is not sourced here.
